note: First verification pass on Chicago, web research from zero (no register). Delivered 3 verified candidates to data/research/chicago-verified.json (chi_001 to chi_003), below the 4-tree floor for a page. leads = trees that failed only on our evidence bar or on the count, raw material for a future pass. blocked = trees that must never ship whatever happens later, each with its reason.

leads.name: University of Chicago Main Quadrangle bur oak / black oak stand
leads.species: Bur Oak (Quercus macrocarpa) and Black Oak (Quercus velutina), mixed stand
leads.location_hint: Humanities Quadrangle and Social Sciences Quadrangle, University of Chicago main campus, Hyde Park, roughly 41.789, -87.5997
leads.why_not_shipped: Two native oak stands predate the University (founded 1890) and were deliberately preserved by trustee Judge Daniel Shorey when the quadrangles were laid out; a Chicago Maroon student column (2019) and a University of Chicago Magazine piece both confirm old oaks still stand in the quads today, and a University Facilities article (paywalled behind the intranet.uchicago.edu React app, could not be fetched by curl or WebFetch in this pass, both redirected to a JS-only shell) reportedly discusses the stand's history in more depth per search-engine summaries only, which is not something to trust without reading the source directly. No confirmed age figure or exact single-tree location was found that would clear the two-source bar for a specific collectible point; the sources describe a stand/cluster across two quads, not one tree with one place to stand. Worth a dedicated pass: visit or find the facilities.uchicago.edu article through a cached/archived copy, or contact UChicago Facilities (contact was named in secondary coverage: Richard Bumstead, associate director of campus environment) to pin an exact specimen and age.
leads.update_2026_08_08: The intranet source was read in a browser session: it quotes Goodspeed's History of the University of Chicago. Key passage: 'Judge Shorey was also the principle advocate for preserving the existing oaks on campus - oaks that in many cases predate the University.' Also: in the University's first year the western side was 'flat, but dry and covered with young oaks', so the preserved oaks were YOUNG in 1892, putting them at roughly 140-170 years now, not ancient. History is now double-sourced; what still fails is the collectible-point rule: every source describes a stand across two quadrangles, no single tree with one place to stand. Only a source naming one individual tree reopens this.

blocked.name: Bur Oak, Lincoln Park Zoo South Lawn
blocked.location_hint: Lincoln Park Zoo, South Lawn, Chicago
blocked.reason: DEAD. This was Chicago's best-known candidate for oldest tree (estimated 250-300 years, predating the city and the USA), but it was removed by crane and chainsaw crews on 2023-05-02 after reaching the end of its life cycle; confirmed by Block Club Chicago, WTTW, NPR and Smithsonian Magazine, all archived. 36 scions were grafted at the Morton Arboretum to preserve its genetics, but the tree itself is gone. Never ship as a living entry.

blocked.name: Birdhouse Oak, Lincoln Park (near Farm in the Zoo)
blocked.location_hint: 1911 N Stockton Dr, Lincoln Park, Chicago, across from the Farm in the Zoo
blocked.reason: Source (Block Club Chicago, 2022) describes it explicitly as a 'dying oak tree' that was given a second life as a public-art bird sanctuary with 190 birdhouses attached, i.e. a snag/dying specimen rather than a living, thriving tree. Fails the 'alive now' bar as reported; would need a fresh 2025/2026 check to see whether it is still standing and whether calling it 'alive' would be honest, or whether it is functionally a dead-tree art installation (which the project's dead-tree rule excludes as a collectible entry regardless of fame).
